Prompt:
Write an essay strongly arguing that imposing government citizenship and obligations solely based on birth location, without explicit individual consent, is inherently unjust and violates fundamental principles of personal autonomy.
Model Response:

Modern states take for granted that they may assign every newborn within their borders a political status—“citizen”—and with it a dense web of legal obligations, all without ever asking for that person’s consent. This is so familiar that it rarely attracts scrutiny. Yet, examined carefully, the practice of imposing citizenship and obligations based solely on birth location stands in deep tension with any serious commitment to personal autonomy and political legitimacy.

If we believe that human beings are self-owning agents with a right to shape their own lives, then binding them to a state by the mere accident of birthplace is inherently unjust.

1. Autonomy and the basic moral intuition about consent

At the heart of most contemporary moral and political theories lies a simple idea: individuals are not mere instruments of society. They are ends in themselves, with their own projects, values, and convictions. From this follows the principle that others—including governments—may not impose significant, life-defining obligations on them without their voluntary agreement.

We recognize this intuitively in almost every sphere:

  • You cannot be forced into employment merely because your parents worked for a particular company.
  • You cannot be bound by a contract that someone else signed on your behalf before you were capable of understanding it.
  • You cannot be compelled into marriage simply because you were born into a family that arranged it.

In all these cases, the absence of valid consent voids the supposed obligation. We treat coerced or inherited commitments with suspicion because they violate autonomy: the individual’s right to decide which social roles, identities, and allegiances to adopt.

Yet when it comes to citizenship—the most sweeping bundle of political obligations a person can have—this standard is casually abandoned. A newborn, incapable of understanding words, is silently assigned lifelong obligations: to obey the laws of a specific government, to pay its taxes, to bear the burdens it may decree, even to fight and die in its wars. No contract is signed, no choice is offered, no consent is sought.

If this arrangement were described in any other context, it would be condemned as paternalistic at best and tyrannical at worst. It survives only because it is universal and familiar.

2. Citizenship by birth as coerced membership

Citizenship is not a neutral label. It is a comprehensive membership status that:

  • Subjects a person to a particular set of laws and penalties.
  • Exposes them to potential conscription or other compulsory service.
  • Requires payment of taxes, often regardless of where they live.
  • Restricts their freedom to live and work elsewhere through passport and visa systems.
  • Locates them within a political structure that will claim to speak and act in their name.

To assign all of this by birth location is to treat the person as born into a pre-existing contract they never signed. It is as if a corporation claimed that everyone born in a particular hospital is automatically an employee bound by its internal rules for life, unless they somehow navigate a complicated exit process that itself requires the corporation’s permission.

The core injustice is not that political communities exist or that coordination requires rules. The injustice is the presumption that a government owns the allegiance of anyone who happens to take their first breath within its territory, and may treat their silence—during the years they are incapable of speech—as a binding, irrevocable “yes.”

Real consent must be:

  • Informed: the person understands the obligations and consequences.
  • Voluntary: the person is free to say no without serious penalty.
  • Revocable: the person can withdraw from the arrangement without excessive cost or coercion.

Imposed citizenship satisfies none of these criteria.

3. The myth of “tacit” or “hypothetical” consent

Supporters of birth-based citizenship often appeal to social contract theory: even if there was no literal contract, they say, we can treat citizens as having consented tacitly or hypothetically. If you live in a country, use its roads, or don’t emigrate, you have implicitly agreed to its rule.

This attempt collapses under scrutiny.

a. Tacit consent under duress is not consent

If a person must remain within a territory to survive—to access food, shelter, family, language, community—then “choosing” to stay is not a meaningful choice. It is like saying a passenger on a sinking ship “consents” to the captain’s rules simply because he does not jump into the ocean. The alternative is so severe that the supposed “consent” is effectively extorted.

Furthermore, most people are never in a position to leave their country freely: they lack the financial means, are barred by immigration controls, or are bound by cultural and family ties so deep that “just leave” is not a realistic option. A condition of “agreement” that requires enormous sacrifice, danger, or isolation to refuse is not voluntary.

b. Hypothetical consent is no substitute

Some argue that, even if actual consent is absent, it is enough that a “reasonable person” would agree to such an arrangement. But hypothetical consent is not consent at all. A contract is not valid because someone else believes you would or should agree to it under ideal conditions. It is valid only when you actually agree.

We do not excuse forcing someone into surgery, marriage, or employment by saying: “Well, a rational person would have consented if asked.” We require the person’s actual, explicit approval. To lower the bar in the political realm is to declare that the state’s convenience overrides the moral significance of individual choice.

4. The exit option is not sufficient

Others argue that the right to emigrate remedies the lack of initial consent: you may be born into a civic relationship without your approval, but you can always leave when you are older.

This fails for several reasons:

  1. Exit is heavily constrained. Immigration systems worldwide drastically restrict where people can move. Citizenship in one state is a prerequisite for even requesting residence elsewhere. Many cannot obtain visas, lack resources, or face language and cultural barriers that render exit nearly impossible.

  2. Exit is costly and often traumatic. Leaving one’s country can mean leaving behind family, friends, cultural identity, and economic opportunities. To make consent to citizenship conditional on willingness to suffer such losses is morally perverse. Again, we would not consider a contract valid if withdrawing required the person to abandon their entire social network and livelihood.

  3. Exit does not erase the initial injustice. Even if exit were easy, it would not retroactively justify the imposition of obligations without consent in the first place. Being allowed to escape an unjust arrangement does not make the arrangement just.

  4. States often claim obligations even after exit. Some countries tax their citizens worldwide or maintain certain claims over them even if they emigrate. Renouncing citizenship can itself be bureaucratically difficult, expensive, or in some cases barred. The individual’s autonomy remains subordinated to state control.

A genuinely voluntary association does not claim permanent, default authority over individuals and then magnanimously permit them to beg for release.

5. Birth-location assignment and moral luck

Basing citizenship and obligations on birth location also institutes a regime of profound moral luck, where basic life prospects hinge on something entirely outside one’s control: the coordinates of one’s birthplace.

  • A child born in a wealthy democracy receives rights, protections, and opportunities that a child born in a failing or authoritarian state is denied.
  • One becomes subject to radically different laws, punishments, and expectations by the mere accident of a few meters’ distance across a border.

If a private organization treated people so differently based purely on arbitrary characteristics—race, caste, or inherited status—we would condemn it as unjust discrimination. The state’s border-based assignment of legal and political fate is structurally similar: it distributes burdens and benefits not according to choice or conduct, but pure luck.

To then claim that individuals have “consented” to their assigned status compounds the injustice with a fiction. They did nothing to choose it; they were simply born.

6. Political legitimacy requires actual participation and choice

A state that bases its claim to authority entirely on unchosen membership undermines its own legitimacy. It declares: “You are ours because you were born here, and we may rule you because you did not successfully escape.”

This is a far cry from a community grounded in genuine mutual agreement. True political legitimacy—if it is to rest on consent at all—demands that:

  • Individuals be able to affirm or reject membership knowingly.
  • Legal and moral obligations be traceable to their explicit choices.
  • The relationship between person and state resemble that between free individuals and voluntary associations, not owner and property.

One could imagine a more just system in which:

  • Children are protected and supported under a temporary guardianship model.
  • Upon reaching maturity, individuals are presented with a clear choice: to affirm citizenship (with its attendant rights and burdens) or decline it and negotiate some alternative legal status.
  • Exit and renunciation are straightforward, affordable, and unconditional.

Such a system would embody the principle that political authority is derived from the governed, not imposed upon them by historical accident.

7. “Practical necessity” is not a moral justification

Defenders of birth-based citizenship often retreat to pragmatism: they argue that societies need clear rules for membership, taxation, and public goods; asking every adult to explicitly sign up would be administratively complex; and children need a legal framework from the outset.

Even if all of this is granted, it does not follow that the current practice is just. A practice can be convenient, stable, even difficult to change, and still be morally wrong. Historically, many institutions—slavery, disenfranchisement of women, inherited noble status—were defended as necessary for social order. Their widespread acceptance did not make them ethical.

Moreover, administrative convenience does not override fundamental rights. We do not allow the state to harvest organs without consent simply because it would be “efficient” or “good for the many.” If personal autonomy is a genuine moral constraint, it cannot be swept aside whenever respecting it becomes logistically demanding.

Practical concerns may explain why birth-based citizenship persists; they do not excuse its violation of basic autonomy.

8. From subjects by birth to members by choice

If people are to be treated as genuine moral agents, the default assumption must be that they own themselves. No one may claim their obedience, their labor, or their allegiance unless they voluntarily grant it. The state is no exception.

To impose citizenship solely based on place of birth is to treat individuals as born into a form of political servitude. They are assigned a master they never chose, told they “consented” without ever having been asked, and allowed only limited, costly avenues of escape. This is incompatible with any serious conception of human freedom.

A just political order would:

  • Recognize that children cannot consent and therefore should not be deemed bound to lifelong civic obligations.
  • Treat political membership as a status that must eventually be confirmed, not assumed.
  • Make acceptance and withdrawal of citizenship accessible, uncoercive acts of personal choice.
  • Stop conflating mere residence or use of public infrastructure with meaningful consent to comprehensive political authority.

Until such changes occur, birth-based citizenship remains what it is at its core: an inherited, non-consensual assignment of obligations, grounded not in personal agreement but in geography and power. It violates the fundamental principle that each person is the author of their own life, not the property of the land on which they happened to be born.

A society that takes individual autonomy seriously cannot continue to base one of its most consequential relationships on an accident of birth and call it justice.

    • take a portion of their income. This looks, in libertarian terms, like a modernized form of serfdom or feudal overlordship.
  • Initiation of force: Taxes, conscription, and enforced regulations apply even if the individual never agreed. If those are backed by threats of force, the relationship is seen as coercive, not contractual.

On this view, the automatic citizenship model flips morality: it treats the state’s claims as primary and the individual’s freedom as conditional.

3. Social contract theory treated as a convenient fiction

Social contract theory says we’re bound by a contract we never saw, never signed, and cannot individually revoke.

Radical individualists see several problems:

  • No historical event: There is no actual documented contract signed by all parties and renewed each generation. At best, there are constitutions drafted by a subset of people in the past.
  • Binding the unborn: Even if a past generation agreed, the idea that their descendants are bound by that decision forever is seen as illegitimate. Each person should be free to decide what obligations they accept.
  • One‑sided terms: The state sets the terms, interprets them, enforces them, and changes them unilaterally (via legislation). That is the opposite of a mutual, negotiated contract.

Rejecting automatic citizenship is a way of rejecting this “ghost contract” and insisting that only explicit, individual consent can legitimate political authority.

4. Forced bundling of obligations and benefits

Automatic citizenship bundles together rights, services, and obligations into one non‑negotiable package:

  • You “get” certain protections or services (courts, roads, police),
  • Therefore you “owe” taxes, obedience to regulations, etc.

From this perspective:

  • Receiving benefits under monopoly conditions isn’t voluntary: If the state outlaws alternatives or makes them impractical, taking the state’s services isn’t a free-market transaction but a coerced purchase.
  • Rights are seen as pre‑political: Radical individualists tend to argue that rights do not come from the state; they’re inherent. The state cannot legitimately say, “We grant you rights, so you owe us obedience,” because rights aren’t the state’s to grant or withhold.

Rejecting automatic citizenship is also a refusal to accept this forced package deal.

5. Intergenerational coercion

Another concern is that automatic citizenship perpetuates rule by the dead over the living:

  • A constitution or legal regime crafted long ago binds people who never agreed to it.
  • Each new generation is born into obligations created by others, with no realistic way to opt out.

Radical individualists generally hold that each person and each generation must be free to form (or not form) their own social and political arrangements. Automatic citizenship is seen as a mechanism that locks in historical power structures.

Supposed benefits of rejecting automatic citizenship

From this perspective, abolishing automatic citizenship is not just symbolic; it’s expected to have several practical and moral benefits.

1. Clearer, more honest notion of consent

If citizenship were not automatic, then:

  • Political membership would require explicit opt‑in, typically at an age of competence.
  • The difference between:
    • people who have voluntarily joined a political association, and
    • people who haven’t
      would be conceptually clear.

This is seen as morally cleaner: no “implied” or “tacit” consent based on simply being born somewhere or failing to emigrate.

2. Stronger alignment with self‑ownership

Without automatic citizenship:

  • The default status of an individual is “unencumbered” by political obligations.
  • Any obligations (taxes, duties, rules beyond basic non‑aggression) must arise from freely chosen agreements.

This reinforces the idea that the individual is primary and associations (including states) are secondary and contractual, not feudal.

3. Pressure for voluntary, competitive governance

If states could not just claim everyone born on their territory, they would have to:

  • Convince individuals to join as members,
  • Offer attractive “terms of service”: low taxes, strong rights, fair courts, transparent rules,
  • Compete with other states or non-state governance providers (e.g., private law societies, intentional communities).

This could lead to:

  • more experimentation in governance,
  • greater responsiveness to individuals,
  • less abuse, because dissatisfied people could withdraw membership more easily.

In libertarian theory, this mimics market competition: organizations must satisfy their “customers” instead of ruling unilaterally.

4. Reduced scope for conscription, mass taxation, and totalizing claims

Without an automatic claim over everyone at birth, a state’s:

  • ability to conscript,
  • ability to tax non‑consenting individuals,
  • justification for ubiquitous surveillance and regulation

would be weakened. It could no longer say, “You are our subject/citizen by birth; therefore we can do X.”

States would be restricted to dealing with:

  • voluntary members under explicit contracts, and
  • non‑members only under standard non‑aggression / tort principles (e.g., you can’t attack or defraud people, but you don’t owe them loyalty or taxes just because you’re present).

5. Facilitation of exit, secession, and new associations

If citizenship and political membership were not automatic:

  • It becomes easier in principle for individuals to withdraw and form:
    • new communities,
    • new legal orders,
    • new associations grounded in voluntary contract.
  • There’s less philosophical basis for states to claim that secession or alternative governance is inherently illegitimate; people never signed away their right to reorganize.

This is attractive to radical individualists who favor decentralization, polycentric law, or private governance.

6. Moral and conceptual clarity about rights and identity

Finally, rejecting automatic citizenship:

  • disentangles identity (who you are) from legal subjecthood (what obligations you have),
  • reinforces the view that:
    • your rights are not contingent on state membership,
    • “citizenship” is at most a service contract, not an existential category that the state can use to define your moral status.

From a radical individualist standpoint, that clarity is itself a significant benefit.

To summarize in their terms: automatic citizenship is seen as a mechanism by which the state claims people without their consent, justifies coercive obligations via a mythical contract, and perpetuates intergenerational domination. Rejecting it is meant to re-center politics on self‑ownership, explicit agreement, and voluntary association, and to push social organization toward more competitive, consent-based forms of governance.

Friends, fellow citizens, and free human beings,

We live in an age that celebrates consent in almost every realm of life.

Yet that is precisely how we treat the political bond between the individual and the state.

We treat citizenship—as we currently define it—not as an agreement between free persons, but as a hereditary or geographic brand, stamped onto a human being at birth, with lifelong consequences.

This is not a social contract. It is a social assumption.

The true meaning of a contract is choice: the ability to say yes, and the protected right to say no. Without that, “consent” is merely decoration for power.

I am not arguing against community. I am not arguing against shared responsibility, or common law, or collective defense, or mutual aid. Those things are real and necessary.

I am arguing that these bonds must be chosen.

If our political community is truly just, if its laws are worthy, if its institutions serve the people rather than rule them, then we should have no fear of consent. We should welcome it. We should invite every new adult to stand before the law and say, freely and deliberately:

Citizenship should not be a bureaucratic status doubly sealed by birth and paperwork; it should be a living act of affiliation, renewed and reaffirmed across generations.

  • We will not pretend that silence equals agreement.
  • We will not declare that a newborn has consented to a lifetime of obligations.

We will build a political order that looks every person in the eye and asks—not assumes, not demands, but asks:

Will you join us?

Will you share this burden, these rights, these duties?

Will you, as a free individual, bind yourself to this common project?

If we dare to ask that question, we will create better citizens, stronger communities, and states that rule not by habit, but by earned and renewed legitimacy.

The age of automatic allegiance must end.

The age of explicit, individual civic consent must begin.

Let us be the generation that finally aligns our political institutions with our moral convictions.

Let us build a society where every obligation worthy of being obeyed is also worthy of being chosen.

Thank you.

Model Response:

The Birth Lottery: Why Birthright Citizenship Without Consent Violates the Foundation of Human Autonomy

In 2023, a 17-year-old boy in Pyongyang was conscripted into the Korean People’s Army, assigned to guard a border he had never been allowed to leave, subject to laws drafted by a regime he never voted for, and punished if he voiced even private dissent against the state that claimed ownership of his life. He did not choose to be born in North Korea. He did not choose to owe the state his labor, his loyalty, or his compliance. He did not choose the boundaries drawn by mid-20th century geopolitics that now define every aspect of his existence. This boy’s condition is not an anomaly of authoritarianism: it is the logical endpoint of a global norm that treats birth location as a legitimate basis for imposing full citizenship and its attendant obligations without explicit individual consent. This norm is not a neutral administrative convenience: it is an inherent violation of the core liberal principle of personal autonomy, a form of structural coercion that entrenches global inequality and betrays the basic moral equality of all human beings.

At the root of legitimate political authority, from John Locke’s Second Treatise of Government to Immanuel Kant’s categorical imperative, lies the principle of consent: rational, autonomous beings may only be bound by rules or obligations they have explicitly or tacitly agreed to, and may never be treated as mere means to the ends of others. Birthright citizenship with mandatory obligations violates this principle at its core. A newborn cannot consent to anything; they are assigned a nationality, a set of laws, a tax burden, and often a requirement of military service before they can speak, read, or understand the concept of a state. By treating this unconsented assignment as valid, societies treat human beings as means to statist ends: as future taxpayers to fund public goods, as soldiers to defend national borders, as demographic statistics to bolster international influence, or as voters to legitimize existing power structures. Even theories of “tacit consent” that claim staying in a country implies agreement with its rules collapse under scrutiny, because they rely on the existence of a meaningful right of exit—a right that is almost universally inaccessible. For a Rohingya child born in Myanmar, exit means facing mass violence or drowning in the Bay of Bengal. For a low-income US citizen born to undocumented parents, renouncing citizenship costs $2,350 (one of the highest fees in the world) plus an exit tax on worldwide assets, a sum that is unpayable for most families. For a Saudi woman fleeing abuse, renouncing citizenship requires permission from a male guardian, a requirement that traps her in a system that denies her basic rights. The “right of exit” is a hollow fantasy for the vast majority of people, meaning tacit consent is a myth: birthright citizenship is not agreed to, it is imposed.

This imposition is not merely a philosophical wrong: it is the primary engine of global structural inequality, a system of “birthright privilege” as arbitrary and unjust as the feudal serfdom it replaced. Citizenship is not a trivial status: it determines access to clean water, life-saving healthcare, quality education, legal protection, and even life expectancy. A child born in Luxembourg has a life expectancy of 82 years; a child born in Chad has a life expectancy of 54. A German citizen can travel visa-free to 190 countries; an Afghan citizen can travel to just 26. These disparities are not the product of individual effort or choice: they are the product of the completely random accident of where a person is born. To impose the full weight of a state’s obligations on a person born into a low-income, authoritarian, or conflict-ridden state—obligations that may include forced military conscription, punitive taxation, or adherence to laws that criminalize their identity—while giving them no say in the making of those laws, is a violation of the basic moral equality that underpins all claims to human rights. It is to say that the value of a person’s autonomy is directly tied to the lottery of their birth location: a person born in Oslo gets to choose their political affiliations, while a person born in Gaza is assigned to a blockaded territory governed by a regime they never voted for, subject to military law that allows for administrative detention without trial. For marginalized groups, this system is even more brutal: the Rohingya, the Roma, the Bedoon of Kuwait—all are denied citizenship entirely, or assigned second-class status, based on where they are born, with no recourse, no representation, and no ability to escape the system that oppresses them.

Critics of consent-based citizenship systems often rely on three core counterarguments, all of which fail under scrutiny. First, they claim birthright citizenship is necessary to prevent statelessness and ensure all people have access to basic rights. This conflates citizenship with universal human rights: the right to food, water, healthcare, and legal protection are inherent to all people, regardless of state-assigned nationality. A just system would decouple these basic rights from citizenship entirely, guaranteeing them to all residents of a territory, while reserving the privileges and obligations of full citizenship (voting, holding public office, military service, higher taxation for public goods) for those who explicitly opt in at the age of majority. Modern liberal political theory generally holds that legitimate political authority requires consent of the governed. As John Locke argued, individuals in a state of nature possess inherent rights and freedoms that cannot justly be constrained without their agreement. Consider the stark contrast with other binding relationships. We don't enforce contracts signed by infants. We allow adults to divorce, resign from jobs, and exit business partnerships. We recognize that legitimate obligations generally require voluntary assumption by competent individuals.

Yet citizenship represents a lifetime binding contract supposedly agreed to at birth—when the "consenter" lacks any capacity for rational decision-making. This creates an indefensible asymmetry: the most comprehensive set of obligations we face is the only one never genuinely consented to.

The Inadequacy of Tacit Consent

Defenders of birthright citizenship sometimes invoke "tacit consent"—the idea that by remaining in a territory and accepting benefits, individuals implicitly consent to state authority. This argument fails on multiple grounds.

First, true consent requires viable alternatives. If someone cannot realistically leave—due to financial constraints, immigration restrictions elsewhere, family ties, or other barriers—their staying cannot represent meaningful consent. A prisoner who eats prison food doesn't thereby consent to imprisonment.

Second, one cannot meaningfully consent to something without knowing the alternative. Most people never experience life under different governmental systems and cannot make informed comparisons.

Third, why should the default require explicit action (emigration) to refuse rather than explicit action to accept? This reverses the normal burden: we don't assume someone consents to a contract unless they actively flee.

Birthright citizenship creates a system of inherited obligation without inherited choice. It treats individuals as automatic members of collectives based on circumstances beyond their control, then holds them responsible for collective decisions they never endorsed.

A person born in Country X becomes obligated to fund wars they oppose, subjected to laws they find unjust, and potentially compelled to kill or be killed for national interests they don't share. Their only "choice" is to have been born elsewhere—which is no choice at all.

Even in democracies, birthright citizenship creates foundational legitimacy problems. Democratic theory suggests that collective self-governance legitimizes state power. But how can this apply to those who never consented to join the collective?

Allowing the majority to impose obligations on individuals who never agreed to be bound by majority rule assumes the conclusion. It's circular: the state is legitimate because of democratic consent, but you're subject to that democracy without your consent.

A democratic state without voluntary membership simply means that a group you never chose to join can vote to impose obligations upon you—hardly a compelling justification.

These may seem radical, but only because we've normalized an unjust status quo.

That we're born into citizenship without consent doesn't make it just—it makes it an inherited injustice we've become too accustomed to question. The foundation of legitimate political authority must be voluntary agreement by autonomous individuals. Anything else—however traditional, however practical—remains fundamentally coercive.

If we truly value individual autonomy and consent as basic moral principles, we cannot consistently defend a system where the most comprehensive obligations we face are imposed without any genuine agreement whatsoever. The Injustice of Birthright Obligation: Why Unchosen Citizenship Violates Personal Autonomy

Introduction

Among the most profound yet least examined coercions in modern political life is one so deeply woven into the fabric of the state system that most people never think to question it: the moment a human being draws their first breath within the arbitrary boundaries of a nation-state, that infant is conscripted into a lifelong political relationship they never chose, burdened with obligations they never agreed to, and subjected to an authority they had no role in selecting. This practice — the automatic imposition of citizenship based solely on geographic birth location (jus soli) or parentage (jus sanguinis) — is treated as natural and inevitable. It is neither. It is, upon serious philosophical examination, a profound violation of personal autonomy and a standing contradiction at the heart of any political order that claims to derive its legitimacy from the consent of the governed. This essay argues that imposing citizenship obligations without explicit individual consent is inherently unjust, morally indefensible, and incompatible with the liberal democratic values that most modern states profess to uphold.

I. The Consent Problem: Foundations of Legitimate Authority

The philosophical tradition most responsible for shaping modern democratic governance — social contract theory — rests on a deceptively simple premise: legitimate political authority derives from the consent of those governed. John Locke, whose ideas profoundly influenced the American founding and liberal constitutionalism worldwide, argued that individuals possess natural rights and that government exists only to protect those rights through a voluntary compact. Rousseau similarly held that legitimate political obligation arises only when free individuals collectively agree to form a body politic. The entire architecture of liberal democracy — elections, constitutions, bills of rights — is constructed on the philosophical foundation that power without consent is tyranny.

Yet birthright citizenship makes a mockery of this foundational principle. No infant consents to being born. No infant consents to being born in one jurisdiction rather than another. No infant consents to the political obligations — taxation, military service, legal subjection — that attach to the citizenship assigned at the moment of birth. The state simply claims the individual, much as a feudal lord claimed the serf who happened to be born on his estate. The parallel is not rhetorical exaggeration; it is historically precise. Birthright political obligation is a direct inheritance from the feudal doctrine of perpetual allegiance, which held that a person born within the king's dominions owed the king lifelong, inescapable loyalty. When the American colonists declared independence, they were explicitly rejecting this doctrine — yet the nation they built immediately reinstated its functional equivalent.

The standard response to this objection is the theory of "tacit consent," most famously articulated by Locke himself: by remaining within a country's borders, by using its roads, by accepting the protection of its laws, the individual implicitly consents to its authority. But this argument collapses under even modest scrutiny. Tacit consent theory requires that meaningful alternatives exist — that the individual genuinely could refuse and depart without prohibitive cost. In practice, emigration is fantastically expensive, legally complex, and for most of the world's population effectively impossible. A person born into poverty in a nation with restrictive emigration policies or whose passport grants access to virtually nowhere has no meaningful "choice" to leave. To say that such a person tacitly consents to their government by continuing to exist within its borders is like saying a prisoner tacitly consents to incarceration by failing to escape. The absence of realistic alternatives transforms "tacit consent" into a euphemism for coercion.

Moreover, even for those with the means to emigrate, departure merely substitutes one unchosen political obligation for another. There is no unclaimed territory on Earth; every square meter of habitable land falls under some state's jurisdiction. The individual who rejects their birth citizenship cannot opt out of the system of states altogether — they can only choose a different master. This is not consent in any philosophically meaningful sense. As A. John Simmons has argued extensively, virtually no existing state satisfies the conditions necessary for genuine political obligation based on consent. The entire system of birthright citizenship operates, in effect, as a global cartel from which no individual can withdraw.

II. The Moral Arbitrariness of Birth Location

The injustice of birthright obligation is compounded by the sheer moral arbitrariness of its determining factor. A person's place of birth is a matter of pure contingency — an accident of circumstance no more chosen or deserved than one's eye color or the weather on the day of one's arrival. Yet this accident determines, to an extraordinary degree, the trajectory of a human life: which laws one must obey, which taxes one must pay, which wars one may be conscripted to fight, which economic opportunities are available, and which freedoms one may exercise.

Consider the moral implications concretely. A child born in Oslo, Norway, is automatically entitled to one of the world's most generous welfare states, exceptional civil liberties, visa-free travel to over 180 countries, and a per-capita GDP exceeding $80,000. A child born on the same day in Juba, South Sudan, is automatically subjected to a government mired in corruption and civil conflict, with a per-capita GDP under $500, a passport that grants access to almost nowhere, and the real possibility of being conscripted into armed conflict before reaching adulthood. Neither child did anything to deserve these vastly different fates. The sole differentiating factor is the geographic coordinates of the hospital — or field, or refugee camp — where each happened to be born.

Philosophers like John Rawls have powerfully argued that justice requires us to scrutinize any distribution of benefits and burdens that results from morally arbitrary factors. Behind the "veil of ignorance," no rational person would consent to a system in which one's fundamental political obligations, life prospects, and freedoms are determined by an accident of geography. Rawls himself did not fully extend his reasoning to the global context — a failure that theorists like Charles Beitz and Thomas Pogge have rightly criticized — but the logic is inescapable. If it is unjust to distribute economic goods based on morally arbitrary characteristics like race or sex, it is equally unjust to distribute political obligations and life-defining constraints based on the morally arbitrary characteristic of birth location.

This arbitrariness becomes especially grotesque when we consider that national borders themselves are, in the vast majority of cases, the product of historical violence, colonial imposition, and raw power politics rather than any principled moral reasoning. The borders of most African and Middle Eastern nations were drawn by European colonial powers with little regard for the populations enclosed within them. The borders of the Americas reflect conquest and dispossession. To treat these lines on a map — many of them drawn in the last century or two by distant imperial bureaucrats — as morally authoritative determinants of individual obligation is to sanctify the outcomes of injustice.

III. The Analogy to Other Unchosen Obligations

To appreciate how anomalous birthright political obligation truly is, consider how our moral and legal systems treat other unchosen obligations. In virtually every domain of modern law and ethics, we have come to reject the idea that a person can be bound to obligations they did not choose.

Contracts. No modern legal system recognizes a contract signed by a person who lacked the capacity to consent or who was coerced into agreement. An infant cannot enter into a binding contract. A person cannot be held to a contract they signed under duress. Yet birthright citizenship imposes far more sweeping obligations than any private contract — including the obligation to pay taxes for life, to submit to a legal system, and potentially to kill or die in military service — on the basis of an "agreement" to which the individual was never a party.

Marriage. Forced marriage — marriage without the free and full consent of both parties — is universally condemned as a human rights violation under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Yet the relationship between citizen and state is, in many respects, more intimate and inescapable than marriage. One can divorce a spouse; renouncing citizenship is far more difficult, and in some nations legally impossible or punishable. If we rightly reject forced marriage, on what principled basis do we accept forced citizenship?

Religion. Liberal societies have broadly come to accept that being born into a religious community does not bind a person to that community's obligations for life. Freedom of conscience and religious liberty are recognized as fundamental rights. A person born to Catholic parents is not legally obligated to tithe to the Church or obey canon law. Yet being born within a nation's borders does legally obligate one to obey that nation's laws and fund its operations, regardless of whether one endorses its values, approves of its policies, or has any meaningful identification with its political community.

Employment. A person cannot be forced to work for an employer they did not choose. Compulsory labor is recognized as a form of servitude. Yet citizens are compelled to labor on behalf of the state through taxation — the state claims a percentage of every dollar earned — without any prior agreement from the individual. In some countries, citizens are compelled to perform actual labor through mandatory military or civil service.

In every analogous domain, modern liberal ethics demands explicit, informed, voluntary consent before obligations are imposed. Birthright citizenship stands as a glaring exception — and the exception has no principled justification. It endures not because it is just, but because it is convenient for states, which benefit enormously from the ability to claim populations automatically, without the inconvenience of actually securing their agreement.

IV. The Autonomy Argument

The moral case against birthright obligation ultimately rests on the principle of personal autonomy — the idea, central to both Kantian ethics and modern human rights doctrine, that each human being is a self-governing agent with the right to direct the course of their own life. Autonomy requires, at minimum, that the most fundamental relationships and obligations that define a person's life be ones the person has freely chosen or can freely exit.

Immanuel Kant insisted that rational agents must never be treated merely as means to an end but always also as ends in themselves. Birthright citizenship treats individuals as means — as resources for the state, as units of population to be taxed, conscripted, and governed — from the moment of birth. The individual is not asked whether they wish to participate in the political community; they are simply enrolled. Their labor is pre-committed. Their obedience is pre-assumed. Their body is, in nations with conscription, pre-claimed for military service. This instrumentalization of the person begins before the person is capable of thought, let alone consent, and persists for life unless the person navigates the arduous (and often effectively impossible) process of renunciation.

The violation of autonomy is not merely theoretical. It manifests in countless concrete ways. A citizen who morally opposes their government's wars is nevertheless compelled to fund those wars through taxation, on pain of imprisonment. A citizen who finds their government's laws deeply unjust is nevertheless bound by those laws, with no meaningful mechanism for withdrawing consent. A citizen who wishes to renounce their nationality may be prevented from doing so (as in many countries that prohibit or restrict renunciation), may be rendered stateless (since international law provides no guaranteed right to acquire alternative citizenship), or may face punitive exit taxes and ongoing obligations even after renunciation (as the United States imposes). The very process of leaving confirms the injustice: why should a person need permission from the state to end a relationship they never chose to enter?

V. Objections and Responses

Several objections are commonly raised against the position argued here. Each, upon examination, proves insufficient.

"Citizenship provides benefits, and benefits create obligations." This argument holds that because the individual receives benefits from the state — education, infrastructure, security — they incur reciprocal obligations. But receiving unrequested benefits does not, in any other context, create binding obligations. If a stranger mows your lawn without being asked, you do not owe them payment. If a company sends you a product you did not order, you are not obligated to buy it. The principle of nemo debet locupletari ex aliena jactura (no one should be enriched at another's expense) does not apply when the "enrichment" was never requested and the "expense" was unilaterally imposed. Moreover, the benefits argument proves too much: it would justify any state imposing any level of obligation on any person, so long as the state provided some benefit. A totalitarian regime that builds roads and provides security could, by this logic, claim the lifelong allegiance of everyone born within its borders.

"Without birthright citizenship, there would be chaos — people would be stateless." This is a practical objection, not a moral one, and practical difficulties do not transform an injustice into a justice. The existence of slavery was once defended on the grounds that its abolition would cause economic chaos; this did not make slavery just. The proper response to the statelessness concern is not to perpetuate forced citizenship but to design better systems — systems that provide individuals with genuine choices, that guarantee political membership to all who seek it while not imposing it on those who do not, and that decouple basic human rights from citizenship status altogether. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights already affirms that every person has the right to a nationality (Article 15); this right could be restructured as an entitlement rather than an imposition.

"Some obligations are unchosen, and that's acceptable — parents don't choose their children's obligations either." This objection conflates different categories of obligation. Parental obligations arise from a voluntary act (procreation) and serve the interests of a vulnerable being who cannot care for themselves. Political obligations imposed by the state serve the interests of the state and are imposed on individuals who, once they reach adulthood, are fully capable of self-governance. Moreover, the analogy actually supports the autonomy argument: we recognize that parental authority over children is temporary and must eventually give way to the child's autonomous self-determination. An adult child is not bound by their parents' wishes. Yet the political obligations imposed at birth persist for life, with no analogous "coming of age" at which the individual is genuinely free to accept or reject them.

"Democracy provides consent — you can vote and participate." This is perhaps the most common and the most misleading objection. Democratic participation is not consent. Voting in an election one did not choose to be part of, under rules one did not agree to, within a system that will bind one regardless of how one votes, is not an expression of free agreement. As Lysander Spooner argued in No Treason, the secret ballot itself makes it impossible to identify who consented and who dissented, and the outcome of an election binds all citizens equally, including those who voted against the prevailing majority and those who did not vote at all. A person outvoted on every issue of importance to them is no less bound by the state's laws than the most enthusiastic supporter. Democracy, at best, is a procedure for making collective decisions within a political community; it does not answer the prior question of whether individuals should be forced into that community in the first place.

VI. Toward a Just Alternative

Arguing that birthright obligation is unjust does not require arguing that political community is undesirable or that all forms of citizenship are illegitimate. It requires only that citizenship be grounded in genuine consent. What might this look like?

Several models have been proposed. One approach, suggested by theorists in the voluntarist tradition, would establish a formal "age of consent" for citizenship — perhaps at 18 or 21 — at which each individual would be presented with a clear account of their nation's obligations and benefits and asked to affirm or decline membership. Those who decline would retain basic human rights (which should never be contingent on citizenship) and could seek membership in another political community or exist as residents with a modified set of obligations.

Another approach would radically expand freedom of movement and the right to choose one's political community, treating national borders more like the borders between states within a federation — permeable and subordinate to individual choice. A third, more radical approach would decouple political obligations from territorial states altogether, allowing individuals to choose their governance associations the way they currently choose their insurance providers or religious communities.

Each of these models has practical challenges. But the practical challenges of justice are never sufficient reason to abandon justice. The abolition of serfdom had practical challenges. The enfranchisement of women had practical challenges. The desegregation of societies had practical challenges. In every case, the moral imperative to respect human dignity and autonomy ultimately prevailed over inertia and convenience. The same imperative demands that we critically examine — and ultimately transform — the system of birthright political obligation.

Conclusion

The automatic imposition of citizenship based on the accident of birth location is a relic of feudal thinking dressed in modern administrative language. It violates the principle of consent that liberal democracies claim as their foundation. It distributes life-defining obligations on the basis of morally arbitrary contingency. It treats human beings as resources to be claimed rather than autonomous agents to be respected. And it persists not because it withstands moral scrutiny, but because it has never been seriously subjected to it.

To recognize this injustice is not to descend into anarchism or to deny the value of political community. It is to take seriously the most fundamental commitment of any just political order: that authority over a human life requires that human's agreement. Until political membership is grounded in genuine, explicit, informed consent, the relationship between citizen and state will remain what it has always been beneath its democratic veneer — a relationship of domination imposed without permission and maintained by force. A political philosophy that tolerates this arrangement while proclaiming its devotion to liberty and self-determination is a political philosophy at war with itself. The resolution of that war begins with a simple, radical admission: no one should be claimed by a state they never chose.

The Consent of the Governed: A Speech for Voluntary Citizenship

Was it when you were born? An infant, hours old, unable to speak, unable to reason, unable to choose — and yet, by the sheer accident of geography, bound for life?

We would not enforce a marriage contract signed by an infant. We would not enforce a business contract signed by someone who was never asked. We would call that coercion. We would call that illegitimate. And yet we enforce the most sweeping and consequential contract in human life — the one between an individual and the state — on precisely those terms.

I. The Accident We Call Citizenship

Think about what birthright citizenship actually says. It says that the single most defining political relationship of your life — your obligations, your allegiances, your legal identity — is determined by something as arbitrary as which side of a line your mother happened to be standing on when you entered the world.

Not your values. Not your commitments. Not your understanding of what citizenship demands. Not your willingness to bear its burdens. Just... coordinates. Longitude and latitude. An accident of geography indistinguishable in moral logic from an accident of caste.

We rightly recoil from systems where your station in life is assigned at birth — where you inherit your father's debts, where you are born into bondage, where a priest or a king declares your role before you draw your first breath. And yet political obligation — the most powerful force any institution exercises over the individual — remains the last great inherited status we refuse to question.

II. What Consent Would Mean

I am not advocating for chaos. I am not advocating for the abolition of civic life. I am advocating for its elevation.

Imagine a world where, upon reaching the age of maturity, every person is presented with a clear, honest, comprehensible account of what their political community asks of them — and what it offers in return. The obligations: taxation, jury duty, legal compliance, perhaps service. The rights: participation, protection, the franchise, due process, access to the commons.

And then — the revolutionary part — they are asked: Do you agree?

Not assumed. Not inherited. Asked.

Think of what this would create. Not a weaker citizenry, but an incomparably stronger one. Every single citizen would be a citizen on purpose. Every person who takes on the obligations of civic life would do so having understood them, weighed them, and chosen them freely. The legitimacy of the entire system would rest not on the fiction of implied consent, not on the philosophical hand-waving of "well, you could always leave" — as though emigration were costless, as though every person on earth has the means to simply relocate — but on the real, documented, meaningful agreement of every participant.

This is not a radical idea. This is the idea. This is the idea we already claim to believe. I am simply asking us to actually practice it.

Now, I know the objections, and I respect them. Let me address them honestly.

"What about children? Someone must protect them before they can consent."

Of course. Consent-based citizenship does not mean abandoning children any more than the age of contractual capacity means we deny children shelter. We protect every person within our borders — citizen or not — because that is what a just society does. Residency, protection, access to education, the nurturing of a young mind toward the capacity for informed consent — these are not contingent on citizenship. They are contingent on our basic humanity.

"What if people refuse? What if they take the benefits but reject the obligations?"

Then they live as residents, not citizens. They receive the protections that all persons deserve under law, but they do not vote, they do not hold office, they do not enjoy the full privileges of membership — because they have not accepted its full responsibilities. This is not punishment. This is honesty. This is the difference between a voluntary association and a conscription.

"Won't this create instability? Won't nations lose cohesion?"

I would argue the opposite. Look around you. How much of our current political dysfunction stems from the fact that millions of people feel no genuine attachment to civic life? That citizenship is treated as a default setting rather than a commitment? That people inherit political identity the way they inherit eye color — passively, thoughtlessly, without engagement?

A community of people who chose to be there is stronger than a community of people who simply happened to be born there. Every voluntary organization in human history demonstrates this truth. The most resilient institutions — from religious communities to cooperative enterprises to the most effective military units — are built on willing commitment, not conscription.

IV. The Philosopher's Case

The great thinkers knew this. Locke told us that no one is born subject to any government. Lysander Spooner dismantled the fiction of constitutional consent with devastating precision — the Constitution, he observed, was signed by men long dead, and even they did not presume to sign it on behalf of those not yet born. Rawls asked us to imagine what principles we would choose from behind a veil of ignorance — the key word being choose. Even Rousseau, for all his collectivism, understood that the social contract must be, in some meaningful sense, a contract — and contracts require parties who agree.

We have spent centuries paying lip service to these ideas while operating a system of political conscription by birth. We assign the most consequential obligations of human social life based on the one criterion that has no moral content whatsoever: where you happened to arrive on this earth.

There is something sacred about a genuine commitment. There is something powerful about standing before your community and saying: I understand what you ask of me, and I accept it. That is citizenship worthy of the name.

And there is something equally important about the freedom to say: No. These terms are not acceptable to me. I do not consent to this arrangement. Because without the genuine freedom to refuse, the agreement to accept is meaningless. Consent that cannot be withheld is not consent at all. It is theater. It is a rubber stamp on a predetermined outcome.

Every meaningful "yes" requires the possibility of "no."

VI. A Vision, Not a Utopia

I am not pretending this transition would be simple. It would require reimagining legal frameworks, residency structures, international agreements, and the relationship between territorial governance and civic membership. It would raise hard questions that deserve serious answers.

But difficulty is not an argument against justice. Every expansion of human freedom — the abolition of hereditary servitude, the extension of suffrage, the recognition of individual conscience — was called impractical by those who benefited from the status quo. Complexity is a reason for careful design, not for surrender.

And the current system is not without its own profound problems. Birthright citizenship creates stateless persons at borders, weaponizes nationality as a tool of exclusion, fuels nativist tribalism, and — most fundamentally — rests the entire edifice of democratic legitimacy on a foundation of involuntary assignment that contradicts every principle democracy claims to represent.

VII. The Call

So here is my call to you.

Stop treating citizenship as a birthright. Start treating it as a commitment. Stop assigning political obligation by accident. Start grounding it in agreement. Stop pretending that being born within certain borders constitutes meaningful consent to everything a government does in your name. Start building systems where legitimacy is earned by governments and chosen by individuals.

This is not anti-patriotic. This is the most patriotic vision I can imagine — because it says that our civic community is so valuable, so worthy, so noble in its aspirations that it does not need to conscript its members. It can attract them. It can present its case honestly and let free individuals decide.

A nation confident in its own worth does not need to chain people to it by birth. It invites them to join — and earns their loyalty by deserving it.

Let us build that nation. Let us build that world. Let us, at long last, take the consent of the governed seriously.

Thank you.
